report.executive_summary: Intel Corporation underwent a transformative restructuring period from 2023 to 2025, shifting from cyclical profitability declines to strategic stabilization driven by state support and asset rationalization. In 2024, the company recorded significant non-cash impairments and restructuring charges totaling approximately $16.3 billion, leading to a reported net loss of $18.8 billion. A pivotal change in 2025 was the reclassification of U.S. government CHIPS Act proceeds as equity proceeds following an SEC accounting objection, which resulted in a $3.0 billion impact to liabilities and equity and contributed to a recovery in reported net income to a loss of only $267 million. Concurrently, Intel executed major capital events, including the divestiture of a controlling stake in Altera for $4.3 billion and a $5.0 billion strategic investment from NVIDIA. These actions, alongside the suspension of dividends due to CHIPS Act restrictions and a reduction in capital expenditures, mark a transition from aggressive global expansion to a capital-efficient, government-supported industrial model with improved liquidity metrics despite continued operating losses.
report.longitudinal_analysis: Disclosure practices shifted significantly across the 2023-2025 period. In 2024, Intel introduced granular disclosures regarding the '2024 Restructuring Plan,' specific legal liabilities from patent settlements ($780 million), and detailed segment revenue attributions. However, this period also saw the removal of quantified geopolitical risk metrics, specifically the disclosure of $3.2 billion in revenue dependent on U.S. export controls. By 2025, the disclosure narrative narrowed, removing specific historical operational risks (such as 10nm/7nm delays and Spectre/Meltdown vulnerabilities) and broad geopolitical warnings, potentially obscuring execution risks. Financial reporting changes in 2025 included the reclassification of CHIPS Act funds from grants to equity proceeds, introducing derivative liabilities, and the deconsolidation of the Altera subsidiary, which materially altered consolidated financial results. The removal of specific CEO transition risks in 2025 indicated the resolution of immediate governance instability.
report.financial_analysis: Financial performance deteriorated sharply in 2024 before stabilizing in 2025. Revenue remained relatively flat, decreasing by 2.08% from 2023 to 2024 ($54.2 billion to $53.1 billion) and holding nearly constant from 2024 to 2025 ($53.1 billion to $52.9 billion). Operating income swung from a near-break-even position of $93 million in 2023 to a massive operating loss of $11.7 billion in 2024, driven by the aforementioned impairments and restructuring costs. This improved to an operating loss of $2.2 billion in 2025. Gross margins contracted significantly from 40.0% in 2023 to 32.7% in 2024, before slightly recovering to 34.8% in 2025. Cash flow from operations declined by 27.8% in 2024 ($11.5 billion to $8.3 billion) but recovered by 17.0% in 2025 to $9.7 billion. Capital expenditures, which had been elevated, decreased sharply by 38.8% in 2025 ($23.9 billion to $14.6 billion). Shareholders' equity declined by 6.0% in 2024 to $99.3 billion but rebounded by 15.1% in 2025 to $114.3 billion, largely due to the equity reclassification of government funds and proceeds from equity transactions. The current ratio improved from 1.33 in 2024 to 2.02 in 2025, reflecting strong liquidity accumulation despite operating losses.

key_findings.title: Massive Non-Cash Charges and Asset Impairments Distorting 2024 Financials
key_findings.analysis: Intel's 2024 financial results were significantly impacted by non-recurring, non-cash charges totaling approximately $16.3 billion. This includes $3.3 billion in non-cash impairments and accelerated depreciation related primarily to the Intel 7 process node manufacturing assets (M0306, M0249), $3.1 billion in goodwill and intangible asset impairments, and $9.9 billion in non-cash tax charges for valuation allowances on deferred tax assets (M0249). These charges fundamentally altered the company's cost structure and profitability metrics, obscuring operational performance without the context of these write-downs.

key_findings.title: Comprehensive 2024 Restructuring Plan and 15% Workforce Reduction
key_findings.analysis: A new material change is the introduction of the '2024 Restructuring Plan,' announced in Q3 2024. This plan involves headcount reductions expected to decrease the core workforce by approximately 15% by early 2025, alongside real estate consolidation and capital rationalization (M0213, M0248, M0334). The company recognized $2.8 billion in restructuring charges associated with this plan (M0248). This represents a strategic shift from the 'limited hiring' and 'rebalancing' mentioned in 2023 to an aggressive downsizing initiative aimed at reducing the cost structure.

key_findings.title: Suspension of Dividends and Buybacks Due to CHIPS Act Restrictions
key_findings.analysis: Capital allocation strategy underwent a drastic change, moving from a reduced dividend in 2023 to a full suspension of dividends starting Q4 2024 and a cessation of stock repurchases (which had already paused in Q1 2021). The disclosure explicitly links the dividend suspension to restrictions under the CHIPS Act commercial agreement, which forgoes dividends for two years with limitations for three years thereafter (M0180). This marks a permanent-seeming shift in shareholder returns driven by regulatory compliance obligations.

key_findings.title: Significant New Legal Liability from Patent Settlements
key_findings.analysis: A new material liability was accrued in Q2 2024 amounting to $780 million for confidential settlement agreements with R2, Third Point, and TRGP regarding patent litigation (M0585). As of December 28, 2024, the remaining unpaid liability was $655 million. This represents a specific, quantified legal expense not present in the prior year's disclosures, impacting the company's restructuring charges and cash flow obligations.

key_findings.title: Removal of Quantified Geopolitical Risk Exposure Metrics
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 filing removes the specific disclosure present in 2023 that quantified $3.2 billion (6% of 2023 revenue) as being dependent on US government export control authorizations due to US-China tensions (M0003). While general risks are discussed, the removal of this specific, high-confidence financial metric represents a significant change in the granularity of disclosed regulatory dependency and financial risk exposure, potentially obscuring the direct revenue impact of current trade restrictions.

key_findings.title: Detailed Segment Revenue Attribution and CHIPS Act Benefits
key_findings.analysis: New disclosures provide granular detail on the Client and Data Group (C&DG) segment, revealing a $1.4 billion revenue decrease in 2024 attributed to lower ASPs and back-end services, partially offset by higher wafer volume from Intel 3, 4, and 7 (M0304). Additionally, the cost of sales increases in 2024 were partially offset by a benefit recognized under the CHIPS Act, highlighting a new revenue/support stream that mitigates operational losses (M0307).

key_findings.title: Material Financial Charges from 2024 Restructuring Plan
key_findings.analysis: In 2024, Intel disclosed significant restructuring costs totaling approximately $2.8 billion, comprising $2.2 billion in employee severance, $442 million in non-cash impairments of construction-in-progress assets, and $103 million in lease-related impairments, along with an additional $83 million in operating lease asset impairments. These charges reflect the financial execution of the 2024 Restructuring Plan, directly impacting the company's 2024 financial position through substantial cash outlays and non-cash asset write-downs related to manufacturing exits and real estate consolidations.

key_findings.title: Significant Goodwill and Intangible Asset Impairments
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 reporting period saw a sharp reversal from previous years' non-impairment conclusions, with Intel recognizing $5.8 billion in total non-cash impairment charges. This includes $3.0 billion in goodwill impairments (largely attributed to the Mobileye reporting unit, where fair value fell below carrying value), a $222 million goodwill impairment for the Intel Foundry unit following segment realignment, and $108 million in acquired intangible asset impairments due to declining cash flow projections. These write-downs signal a material decline in the valuation of acquired entities and strategic business units.

key_findings.title: Cessation of Capital Returns and Credit Deterioration
key_findings.analysis: Intel fundamentally altered its capital allocation strategy in 2024 by suspending its quarterly dividend in Q4 and agreeing to forgo dividends for two years under a CHIPS Act agreement, effectively ceasing all capital returns to stockholders. Concurrently, total debt increased to $51.0 billion, and multiple credit rating downgrades occurred in 2024 due to cyclical revenue pressures and debt service requirements, increasing borrowing costs and limiting future capital access compared to the 2023 status.

key_findings.title: Major Strategic Capital Events: CHIPS Act Awards and Ireland SCIP Transaction
key_findings.analysis: 2024 introduced two major capital structure events. First, Intel secured up to $10.9 billion in CHIPS Act direct funding, receiving $3.0 billion for the Secure Enclave program and signing a $7.9 billion agreement, with $2.2 billion in cash received across 2024 and 2025. Second, the company raised $11.0 billion in net proceeds by selling a 49% interest in its Ireland SCIP entity to Apollo Global Management, marking a significant strategic partnership and capital resource event involving variable interest entity (VIE) consolidation dynamics.

key_findings.title: Resolution of Long-Standing European Commission Litigation
key_findings.analysis: In October 2024, the Court of Justice dismissed the European Commission's appeal regarding a 2009 competition matter, upholding the General Court's annulment of the original findings and the associated €1.1 billion fine. This final resolution removed a significant legal contingency that had been pending in prior filings, confirming the return of funds to Intel and closing a major regulatory overhang.

key_findings.title: Settlement of European IP Litigation
key_findings.analysis: In August 2024, Intel disclosed the resolution of the German injunction enforcement risk and related litigation involving R2 Semiconductor, Third Point, and TRGP Capital. This involved a significant cash outflow of approximately $780 million across three confidential agreements. The settlement aimed to ensure business continuity in Europe by resolving pending litigation and providing broad-based litigation peace, including rights to other technology and services.

key_findings.title: Deterioration of 2023 Financial Performance Disclosed in 2023 Filing
key_findings.analysis: The 2023 Form 10-K highlighted a sharp decline in profitability, reporting an operating loss of $530 million for the total company in 2023 compared to $1.3 billion in operating income in 2022. Additionally, specific segment reporting indicated an operating loss of $482 million for a particular segment (compared to $1.0 billion income in 2022). The filing also noted that customer incentives designed to accelerate purchases and gain market share contributed approximately $700 million to Q4 2023 revenue, impacting future guidance.

key_findings.title: Introduction of U.S. Government Equity Stake and CHIPS Act Risks
key_findings.analysis: The 2025 filing introduces significant risks associated with the U.S. government's acquisition of equity interests in Intel. Disclosed risks include the potential invalidation of transactions by U.S. branches, the elimination of future CHIPS Act and Secure Enclave grant funding, stockholder dilution, reduced voting rights for other shareholders, and adverse impacts on non-U.S. business due to foreign regulations or restrictions.

key_findings.title: SEC Accounting Objection and Revision of Secure Enclave Revenue Treatment
key_findings.analysis: In December 2025, Intel disclosed that the SEC staff objected to its accounting treatment of Secure Enclave program receipts, which it had previously classified as government grants. Intel revised its accounting in Q4 2025 to classify these receipts as equity proceeds. This revision increased the derivative liability fair value to $2.7 billion and resulted in a $3.0 billion impact to liabilities and equity on the balance sheet.

key_findings.title: Strategic Equity Investment from NVIDIA
key_findings.analysis: Intel completed a private placement transaction with NVIDIA in December 2025, selling 215 million shares of common stock for an aggregate price of $5.0 billion. The shares were issued at $23.28 per share under an agreement dated September 15, 2025. This transaction represents a major capital raising event and strategic alignment with a key competitor and customer.

key_findings.title: Removal of Historical Process Technology and Product Defect Risks
key_findings.analysis: Comparing disclosures between 2023/2024 and 2025, Intel removed specific references to historical operational and product risks. The 2023 filing explicitly warned about delays in 10nm and 7nm process technologies and complexity in disaggregated design. The 2024 filing detailed specific product vulnerabilities (Spectre/Meltdown) and instability issues with Core 13th/14th Gen processors. These specific risk disclosures were absent in the 2025 filing, potentially indicating a shift in risk narrative or compliance with new disclosure norms.

key_findings.title: Reduction in Specific Geopolitical and Macroeconomic Risk Disclosures
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 filing provided detailed disclosures on geopolitical risks, specifically citing tensions in China, Taiwan, Ukraine, and Israel, and their impact on supply chains (particularly Taiwan-dependent components) and sales. These specific, high-level geopolitical risk factors and macroeconomic condition warnings were removed from the 2025 filing's disclosed risk sections, representing a significant change in the granularity of operational risk reporting.

key_findings.title: CEO Retirement and Removal of Leadership Transition Risk
key_findings.analysis: In 2024, Intel disclosed specific risks associated with the retirement of its CEO in December 2024 and the resulting leadership transition. In the 2025 filing, this specific narrative was removed, though general talent retention risks remain. This removal indicates the resolution of the immediate governance instability, though the absence of the event-specific disclosure may obscure ongoing succession planning details or residual transition risks from the governance perspective.

key_findings.title: Expansion of Asset Impairments and Operational Consolidations
key_findings.analysis: Intel updated its financial impairment charges, reflecting $3.3 billion in 2024 and $950 million in 2025, driven by reassessed demand and constrained capital. The 2025 disclosure expands the scope of operational disruptions by explicitly adding the cancellation of manufacturing projects in Ohio, Germany, Poland, Malaysia, and Israel, as well as the consolidation of the Costa Rica assembly facility. This signals deepening capital constraints and a strategic pullback on global expansion plans compared to the 2024 focus on delays.

key_findings.title: Intel 18A Node Moves from Planning to High-Volume Manufacturing
key_findings.analysis: The disclosure regarding Intel 18A process technology shifted from a forward-looking expectation of high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in 2025 to a confirmed statement that HVM commenced in late 2025. The first product, Core Ultra Series 3, was released in 2025 using this node, which features gate-all-around transistors (RibbonFET) and backside power delivery (PowerVia). This marks a critical execution milestone, transitioning the company from development to commercialization of its most advanced leading-edge node, which is central to its competitive strategy.

key_findings.title: Divestiture and Deconsolidation of Altera Subsidiary
key_findings.analysis: Intel executed a major strategic shift by selling 51% of its wholly-owned subsidiary, Altera, in September 2025 for $4.3 billion, deconsolidating it from its financial statements and treating the retained interest as an equity method investment. This action, previously only discussed as a potential monetization opportunity in 2024, materially alters Intel's operational scope, capital structure, and consolidated financial results, reducing its exposure to the programmable logic market while generating significant cash proceeds.

key_findings.title: Strategic Risk to Intel 14A Development Based on External Demand
key_findings.analysis: Intel introduced a conditional risk for its Intel 14A process node, stating it may pause or discontinue the development of next-generation leading-edge technologies if a significant external foundry customer is not secured. This represents a departure from the 2024 disclosure, which presented 14A as an active development program with expected improvements. The new disclosure highlights the high capital intensity of the foundry business and the critical dependency on external demand to justify further R&D investment, adding significant uncertainty to the future product roadmap.

key_findings.title: Enactment of 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' Changing Tax Landscape
key_findings.analysis: In July 2025, the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' was signed into law, permanently extending key elements of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, including 100 percent bonus depreciation and modifying the AMIC credit rate. This new regulatory change replaces the general risk factors regarding potential tax law changes disclosed in 2024, materially impacting Intel's future tax obligations and strategic planning environment by providing greater certainty and potential incentives for domestic investment.

key_findings.title: U.S. Government Agreement: Equity Issuance in Exchange for CHIPS Act Funding
key_findings.analysis: Intel entered into a new agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce in August 2025, accelerating $5.7 billion in CHIPS Act disbursements and securing $3.2 billion for the Secure Enclave program. In exchange, Intel issued 433 million shares (including escrowed shares) and warrants for up to 241 million shares to the government. This new disclosure introduces a massive equity dilution event and significant government stake obligations, fundamentally changing Intel's capital structure and relationship with the U.S. government compared to the 2024 filing, which only described the initial entry into the funding agreement with milestone restrictions.

key_findings.title: Enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act alters long-term tax structure
key_findings.analysis: In 2025, Intel disclosed the enactment of the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' on July 4, 2025. This legislation permanently key elements of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, specifically maintaining 100% bonus depreciation and domestic research cost expensing, while increasing the Alternate Minimum Income Tax (AMIT) to 35% from 25%. The provisions have phased effective dates extending through 2027. This is a material change as it directly dictates Intel's future tax liabilities, cash flows, and strategic tax planning capabilities for the long term.

key_findings.title: Completion of Altera divestiture generates $4.3B proceeds and $5.6B pre-tax gain
key_findings.analysis: In 2025, Intel completed the divestiture of a 51% controlling stake in Altera. The transaction resulted in $4.3 billion in net purchase consideration, comprising immediate cash proceeds and deferred payments, with $4.2 billion in net cash proceeds recognized in investing activities. Financially, this resulted in a $5.6 billion pre-tax gain, of which $2.1 billion stemmed from the remeasurement of the retained equity investment. This significantly impacted the 2025 income statement and provided substantial liquidity.

key_findings.title: Finalization of NAND memory business sale to SK hynix resolves contingencies
key_findings.analysis: The 2025 disclosures mark the completion of the second phase of Intel's NAND memory business sale to SK hynix on March 27, 2025. This event allowed Intel to collect the outstanding $2.0 billion receivable and settle pending penalties and contingencies related to the manufacturing and sale agreement. While the settlement resulted in $229 million in net charges, it eliminated significant future cash exposure and legal risk associated with the prior pending transaction status described in 2024.

key_findings.title: Mobileye goodwill impairment reversal indicates improved valuation outlook
key_findings.analysis: A significant change in financial reporting occurs regarding the Mobileye reporting unit. In Q3 2024, Intel recognized a $2.8 billion non-cash goodwill impairment charge due to fair value falling below carrying value. By Q4 2025, despite continued declines in market capitalization, Intel's quantitative impairment assessment determined that no impairment charge was recognized because the estimated fair value exceeded the carrying value. This reversal or non-recognition materially alters the reported financial condition and asset valuation for the segment.

key_findings.title: US Government Agreement proceeds classified as derivative liability
key_findings.analysis: In Q3 2025, Intel received $5.7 billion in proceeds from the U.S. Department of Commerce. The initial accounting classification treated the escrowed shares as a derivative liability recorded at fair value, with subsequent changes flowing through operations. The remaining proceeds were allocated to common stock and warrants. This introduces a significant derivative liability component to Intel's financial structure that was not present in prior periods, establishing the basis for future fair value adjustments.

key_findings.title: Removal of specific operational risk and industry trend disclosures reduces transparency
key_findings.analysis: The 2025 filing removes several material qualitative disclosures present in 2024. Specifically, it omits historical details on semiconductor development delays (10nm/7nm) and the $922 million Gaudi AI inventory charge. Additionally, detailed macro-level analysis of industry shifts (monolithic to chiplets) and specific export control impacts (including Chinese competition and SMIC investments) have been removed. The 2025 filing also removes the specific disclosure that Intel Foundry external revenue decreased 60% in 2024. These removals reduce the granularity of disclosed execution risks, competitive threats, and segment performance drivers.

materiality.reason: The disclosure details a significant $4.1B increase in Cost of Sales, explicitly attributing $3.3B to non-cash impairments and accelerated depreciation of manufacturing assets (Intel 7). This is a material change in financial position and operational reality, disclosing major asset write-downs and strategic execution risks (Intel 7 node issues) not present in the previous year's disclosures.
materiality.key_change: Disclosure of $3.3B impairment/depreciation charges on Intel 7 assets

sources.text: Cost of sales was $25.6 billion in 2024, up $4.1 billion from 2023, primarily driven by higher period charges related to non-cash impairments and accelerated depreciation of $3.3 billion for certain manufacturing assets, a substantial majority of which related to our Intel 7 process node; higher intersegment cost of goods sold of $1.3 billion primarily driven by higher sales volume and higher costs from the ramp of advanced technologies; and higher period charges primarily related to factory start-up costs.

materiality.reason: Introduction of a new $780 million accrual for confidential settlement agreements with R2, Third Point, and TRGP. This represents a significant new legal liability and cash outflow obligation arising from the resolution of specific patent litigation, which was not present or finalized in the 2023 filing.

sources.text: In addition, in the second quarter of 2024, we accrued a charge of $780 million within restructuring and other related to three separate confidential settlement agreements with R2, Third Point, and TRGP (see R2 Semiconductor Patent Litigation below).

materiality.reason: The 2023 disclosure provided a specific, quantified financial exposure ($3.2 billion, 6% of revenue) dependent on US government export control authorizations due to US-China tensions. The removal of this specific metric and the associated detailed risk description from the 2024 filing represents a significant change in disclosed financial risk exposure and regulatory dependency, which is highly material to the financial position.
materiality.key_change: Removal of quantified export control dependency and geopolitical risk

sources.text: In particular, geopolitical and trade tensions between the US and China, one of our largest markets, have led to increased tariffs and trade restrictions, including tariffs applicable to some of our products, and have affected customer ordering patterns.
Further, the US has imposed restrictions on the export of US-regulated products and technology to certain Chinese technology companies, including certain of our customers.
Specifically, in 2022 the US significantly increased US export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment and on artificial intelligence and advanced computing products.
In 2023, the US added to the restrictions in all three areas and also worked with Japan and the Netherlands to align on additional restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
During this time, the US has increasingly added Chinese companies to prohibited lists.
In response, China has restricted US access to certain minerals and has blocked certain companies that provide products to Taiwan's military from selling products in China.

These restrictions have in some instances reduced our sales and in a number of instances required specific governmental authorizations or exceptions - $3.2 billion, or 6%, of our 2023 revenue was dependent upon US government export control authorizations, an amount that we expect may increase in future years.
These and potential future restrictions could adversely affect our financial performance and result in reputational harm to us.

materiality.reason: The disclosure changes from a statement of a 'reduced quarterly dividend' to a full 'suspension' of dividends and a cessation of repurchases, explicitly linking this to CHIPS Act restrictions. This represents a material change in the company's financial position, liquidity strategy, and regulatory compliance obligations.
materiality.key_change: Suspension of dividends and repurchases due to CHIPS Act

sources.text: Our capital allocation strategy includes returning excess cash to stockholders.
We achieve this through our dividend policy and, when permissible, stock repurchases.
In 2023, we declared a reduced quarterly dividend on our common stock.

This dividend reduction reflects our deliberate approach to capital allocation, is expected to support the critical investments needed to execute our business strategy, and is designed to position us to create long-term value.
Our capital allocation strategy historically included returning excess cash to stockholders through dividends and stock repurchases.
Our most recent stock repurchase was in the first quarter of 2021 and we suspended the declaration of quarterly dividends starting with the fourth quarter of 2024.
We agreed under our commercial CHIPS Act agreement to forgo paying dividends for the next two years, and agreed to limitations on the payment of dividends for the three years thereafter.

Further, we do not expect to pay dividends or make stock repurchases until our cash flows improve as we focus on the critical investments needed to execute our business strategy and create long-term value.

sources.text: In 2024, we announced our intention to implement a series of cost and capital reduction initiatives designed to adjust our spending to current business trends while enabling our new operating model and continuing to fund investments in our core strategy-returning to product and process competitiveness.

These initiatives, which we refer to as our 2024 Restructuring Plan, include reducing headcount, consolidating and reducing our global real estate footprint, conducting portfolio reviews of our businesses under a "clean sheet" view, rationalizing capital investments and deployments based upon demand signals and capacity requirements, and reducing our overall operating expenses.
The headcount actions in connection with the 2024 Restructuring Plan are expected to result in an approximate 15% decrease in our core Intel workforce by early 2025.
As a result of initiating and deploying our 2024 Restructuring Plan, we recognized restructuring charges of $2.8 billion in 2024.

sources.text: Our quarterly qualitative impairment assessment for the third quarter of 2024 indicated that a more detailed quantitative analysis was necessary for certain of our reporting units, primarily due to the decline in our market capitalization below the carrying value of our net assets, as well as the decline in our Mobileye reporting unit's market capitalization below the carrying value of Mobileye's net assets.
Our quantitative assessment was performed by measuring each reporting unit's fair value using the income approach, the market approach, or a combination of both.
When using the income approach, we tested the reasonableness of the inputs and outcomes of our discounted cash flow analysis against available market data.

As a result of our impairment tests, we recognized a non-cash goodwill impairment charge of $2.8 billion in the third quarter of 2024 within restructuring and other, most of which related to our Mobileye reporting unit, as the estimated fair value of the reporting unit was lower than the assigned carrying value.

During the fourth quarter of 2025, we completed our annual goodwill impairment assessment across all of our reporting units and identified that a more detailed quantitative analysis was necessary for our Mobileye reporting unit, primarily due to the decline in Mobileye's market capitalization below the carrying value of Mobileye's net assets.
Our quantitative assessment was performed by measuring Mobileye's fair value using the income approach.
When using the income approach, we tested the reasonableness of the inputs and outcomes of our discounted cash flow analysis against available market data.
As a result of this impairment test, no impairment charge was recognized as the estimated fair value was higher than the assigned carrying value.
